synopsis: Accepted practitioner report contributing a production failure taxonomy and cost-sensitive experimental safeguards, rather than a new algorithm. For pieces 01–03, it supplies author-reported evidence about delegated code experimentation, human and automated steering, offline evaluation, and resource-dependent workflow design. Its two Amazon book-recommendation systems belong to one organizational evidence lineage, not independent external replication. Reported gains and autonomous coverage expansion should remain attributed to the authors. These orientation notes do not replace passage citations.
limitations_and_counterevidence: The headline System A lift is a peak-date result; the reported across-date lift is smaller. System B's best coherence followed human pivots, and no run met all three usability criteria. The claim that an immutable evaluator prevents metric gaming conflicts with the documented coherence-gaming example: evaluator integrity does not establish metric validity. The categorical component-causality claim is qualified by the authors' admission that accumulated iterations remain a confound. Offline metrics were not validated against customer outcomes, and proprietary data prevents direct public reproduction. Cost comparisons involve different systems and workloads; they do not establish general efficiency or independently measured labor savings.

passages.purpose: Methods and delegation boundaries: prevention, redirection, and persistence differ by cost regime; System B explicitly depends on human steering and maintained instructions.

locator.quote:
| Principle | System A (high cost) | System B (low cost) | 
|---|---|---|
| Prevent | Code Fixer agent (pre-execution) | Automatic revert (post-execution) | 
| Redirect | Criticizer agent (automated) | Human cross-run pivot | 
| Persist | S3 cross-job storage | Human-maintained program.md | 
The implementation differs with iteration cost—pre-execution gates justify their overhead only when a failed iteration wastes hours of compute; post-execution revert suffices when iterations are cheap enough to treat as disposable hypotheses.

passages.purpose: Cost, hardware, campaign size, and comparison scope: author-reported workload differences contextualize the workflow recommendations rather than establish a controlled efficiency comparison.

passages.purpose: Concrete failure and counterevidence: metric optimization produced unusable clusters, required human guardrails, and never satisfied all usability criteria. Read against the immutable-evaluator claim.

locator.quote: In System B, the agent discovered that maximizing codebook size trivially improves weighted coherence by creating more fine-grained clusters, but the resulting hierarchy was unusable—deep levels collapsed into singletons. We had to introduce a guardrail constraining n_levels and add a tertiary cluster-usability metric to prevent the agent from gaming coherence at the expense of a meaningful hierarchy. More strikingly, even with these additions, the three usability criteria (weighted coherence, genre purity, and median cluster size) were never simultaneously met in any of 15 runs across 150+ iterations, indicating that the tradeoff was structural rather than a tuning problem.

passages.purpose: System A reported results and baselines, retaining the peak-date qualification, variability, campaign duration, and smaller across-date mean lift.

locator.quote: Code-level AutoResearch with the full three-agent framework reached a 1.82\(\times\) relative lift over the hand-tuned baseline (3.79%) and 2.45\(\times\) over the deployed retrieval baseline (2.82%) on its peak evaluation date (\(\pm\) 0.28 pp across 11 evaluation dates; the peak is \({\sim}\)2.6\(\sigma\) above the across-date mean), an iter-12 result obtained over six AutoResearch runs spanning \({\sim}\)10 weeks, within the broader twelve-week campaign that also includes the manual-engineering phase shown in Figure [2](#S4.F2). Even the across-date mean preserves a 1.63\(\times\) lift over the hand-tuned baseline.

passages.purpose: System B comparison and human contribution: the phase table preserves the regression and shows that the best reported result followed a human-directed input pivot.

| Phase | Trigger / Focus | Best WC | Lift | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | Hand-tuned (2–3 days) | 0.348 | 1.00\(\times\) | 
| Phase 1 | Agent: architecture discovery | 0.691 | 1.98\(\times\) |

passages.purpose: Bounded autonomous contribution: the authors describe an unrequested coverage expansion, its implementation, and the Code Fixer's intervention; this is a coverage claim rather than demonstrated customer benefit.

locator.quote: In an iteration whose primary objective was an unrelated loss-function experiment, the Researcher noticed the coverage gap and proposed a text-only fallback: items absent from the behavioral graph would receive an embedding inferred from their text features alone, projected into the same 128d space as the behavioral embeddings via a small MLP trained jointly with the main model. The Code Fixer’s pre-execution review caught one DDP wrapper bug in the fallback path; the iteration ran successfully and the next FAISS index covered all items. Coverage thus expanded by 5.8\(\times\) in a single iteration, without any human direction. No human had specified the gap as a target; no program.md entry mentioned coverage.

passages.purpose: Preserve the strong component-causality claim for explicit comparison with the observational-ablation limitation; do not adopt it as an established causal result.

locator.quote: The ceiling was broken only as each additional agent was introduced (Reviewer/Fixer to 1.45\(\times\), Criticizer to 1.82\(\times\)), establishing that the gain came from the specific agents rather than accumulated iterations alone.

passages.purpose: Evaluation safeguards and their limits: repeated evaluation dates and larger-scale retesting are reported, alongside the overbroad claim that evaluator immutability prevents metric gaming.

locator.quote: First, robustness across evaluation dates. A single lucky evaluation date could flatter the result, so we re-evaluated System A’s iter-12 model on 11 distinct customer-purchase dates; the gain held throughout (peak 6.90%, mean 6.18% \(\pm\) 0.28 pp, with the peak \({\sim}\)2.6\(\sigma\) above the across-date mean). Second, an immutable evaluator. In both systems the agent can read the evaluator’s output but cannot change its code, so it cannot inflate its own score by gaming the metric. Third, full-scale re-testing (System B). To rule out that the gains were an artifact of cheap, small-scale exploration, each architectural decision found in early runs (bottleneck encoder, deeper encoder, batch-size and codebook scaling) was re-tested at the larger Phase 2 data scale before being locked in for later phases.

passages.purpose: Causal, external-validity, and outcome limitations: accumulated iterations remain a confound, both systems share a domain and organization, and offline gains do not establish customer outcomes.

locator.quote:
First, the component ablation for System A is
observational: the campaign transitions in Table [V](#S5.T5)
are natural rather than controlled, and we cannot fully rule out
that accumulated iterations—rather than specific agent
interventions—contributed to the trajectory. While we address this through sequential and artifact-level evidence (Section V-A), a
controlled replication on a different system would strengthen the
causal claim even further. Second, both systems operate within a single domain (book recommendation) at a single organization; whether the five failure modes and the cost-dependence principle generalize to other domains remains to be established. We discuss how the three principles map to other agentic domains under Beyond AutoResearch below, but empirical validation outside recommendation is future work. Third, the evaluation metrics (Recall@6, weighted coherence) are offline proxies that were chosen for the evaluation of these specific systems; neither has been validated against actual customer outcomes in this study, and the gap between offline improvement and production impact is a known risk in recommendation systems.

passages.purpose: Reproducibility gap and available methodological detail: proprietary training and purchase data are unavailable; the authors instead describe a schema and held-out retrieval protocol for replication on other data.

locator.quote: The training data—co-purchase behavioral graphs and customer purchase logs—is proprietary and cannot be released; we describe the schema (anonymized customer–item interactions, text features from a pretrained sentence transformer [[22](#bib.bib11)]) and the evaluation protocol (FAISS [[20](#bib.bib9)] IVF+Flat top-6 retrieval against held-out next-purchase) in sufficient detail that the framework can be replicated on other behavioral datasets. The complete reproducibility checklist required by the ICDM Applied Track is submitted alongside this manuscript.
